data_flow: Unauthenticated POST customer_id_for_subscriptions and subscriptions_id_for_subscriptions (sanitize_text_field only, no nonce or capability check) -> Setting::lookingForSubscription (lib/Setting.php:6281-6370) sends them to the vendor API, then writes the returned subscription fields to plugin options and sets the subscription status to Active.

Editor-level POST value -> stripslashes -> file_put_contents to the uploads directory as front_end.css / front_end.js with no sanitisation, and that file is loaded on public pages, so script content can be stored for every visitor. Gated by edit_others_posts or the plugin's manager/editor roles, not by a manage_options check.

The shortcode front end emits nonce_download to every visitor (index.php:1484, localizeScript at index.php:5616); a POST to admin-ajax.php with that nonce passes the wp_verify_nonce check at index.php:5307 because the capability gate at 5300 is skipped under DOING_AJAX, and the request then runs Schedule.php:7260 getDownloadCSV, which reads $_POST parameters and has no capability check, and returns the booked-customers CSV.

$_POST['customer_id_for_subscriptions'] and $_POST['subscriptions_id_for_subscriptions'] pass only sanitize_text_field and no nonce or capability check, then reach Setting.php:6281 lookingForSubscription, which sends them to the remote license service (6306), stores the returned values as _prefix options (6336-6344) and sets the subscription status to Active (6350).

$_POST['value'] (editor-level, nonce-protected via wp_ajax_booking_package at index.php:4455) goes through stripslashes at 6065 and file_put_contents at 6066 into the uploads plugin directory as front_end.js, so script written by a role below administrator is stored for later loading in other users' browsers. The minimum role is editor (edit_others_posts), which the admin tier label covers.

$_POST['key'] (editor-level, nonce-protected) becomes the option name after sanitize_text_field at Setting.php:2831, and update_option($key, $token) at 2841 overwrites any wp_options entry with a generated hash, with no allowlist of permitted keys.

Public shortcode page localizes nonce_download (index.php:5616 via localizeScript called at index.php:1484) -> visitor POSTs it to admin-ajax.php -> getDownloadCSV only checks capabilities for the download decision, and when DOING_AJAX is true it proceeds with only wp_verify_nonce($_POST['nonce'], action_control.'_download') as the gate (index.php:5300-5307) -> Schedule.php:7260 getDownloadCSV queries booked_customers rows and returns CSV (index.php:5326).

$_POST['customer_id_for_subscriptions'] and $_POST['subscriptions_id_for_subscriptions'] (only isset checks and sanitize_text_field, no nonce or capability check, index.php:5337-5340) -> Setting.php:6281 lookingForSubscription, which sends them to the remote extension server and writes returned values into plugin options via update_option (Setting.php:6336-6338).

$_GET['ical'] and $_GET['site'] reach isValid() unauthenticated; the token is compared with loose == against the ical_token option or a calendar account's icalToken, which Schedule.php:3632 generates as hash('ripemd160', date('U')) (second-resolution timestamp, so guessable). The siteToken is sent to the front-end script (index.php:5811). On a match, the iCal body with customer names and form data is printed (Ical.php:40, 56).

The nonce_download value is printed to every visitor by localizeScript (index.php:5616) on the public booking_package shortcode page (index.php:1484). getDownloadCSV (admin_init, index.php:345) skips the capability gate whenever DOING_AJAX is true, then checks only $_POST['nonce'] against package_app_action_download, and the sink is Schedule::getDownloadCSV (lib/Schedule.php:7260), which builds the booked-customers CSV for a POST-supplied accountKey and month/year with no capability check.

$_POST['key'] (only gated by edit_others_posts or plugin manager/editor roles in selectedMode, index.php:4478) is passed through sanitize_text_field into refreshToken and used directly as the name of an option in update_option($key, $token) at lib/Setting.php:2841, so a non-admin editor-level user can overwrite any site option, including core options, with a random hash.
option license_key -> WS_Form_Common::get_license_key_obscured() (last 6 characters kept) -> returned in JSON 'license' field of api_test with no capability check

Public POST /submit/ field value -> WS_Form_Submit_Meta::db_update_from_array stores it unchanged as meta_value (class-ws-form-submit-meta.php:261, only arrays are serialized) -> db_get_submit_meta calls unserialize() when is_serialized() is true (class-ws-form-submit.php:1061) with no allowlist of classes.

Route permission_callback returns true (api/class-ws-form-api.php:166) -> api_test reads the stored license_key option via WS_Form_Common::get_license_key_obscured (class-ws-form-common.php:4979-4988) and returns its last six characters in the response.

Contributor-authored shortcode attribute file (also data_file, attachments, page_background, conversion_config_file, client_certificate) -> eval_shortcode stores it in encrypted custom_options -> save_as_pdf_pdfcrowd decrypts it (1636-1647) -> prepare_conv 1245-1268 places it in $files without path checks -> build_body 1107 file_get_contents() reads any server-readable path and uploads its content to api.pdfcrowd.com, with the result returned to the visitor who clicks the button.

Contributor-authored shortcode attribute url, with conversion_mode set to a non-url value (e.g. upload) -> stored in encrypted custom_options -> decrypted in save_as_pdf_pdfcrowd (1636-1647) -> do_post_request 1172-1193 passes $options['url'] to get_url() -> wp_remote_get() at line 993 with no scheme, host or private-address restriction, so the server fetches an arbitrary URL and the fetched HTML is rendered into the returned PDF.

Contributor-set shortcode attribute 'url' goes to custom_options at eval_shortcode 940-957 and is encrypted at 865-868; the visitor's nopriv request decrypts it at 1636-1646 and do_post_request 1191 passes it to get_url, which calls wp_remote_get() at 993 with no wp_safe_remote_get or host validation, so the server fetches an attacker-chosen URL (including internal hosts) and returns the body inside the PDF.

Contributor-supplied attrs 'button_indicator_html' and 'button_indicator' go into $options at line 949; for a non-unfiltered_html post author the sanitizer at 929-932 runs wp_kses_post on 'button_custom_html' instead of 'button_indicator_html', so the raw value reaches create_button_from_style where it is concatenated unescaped into the button markup at 735-737 and output to every visitor.

When the email_recipient setting is 'prompt' (set by an admin or via a contributor's shortcode attribute), the anonymous request's $_POST['recipient'] is returned without validation at 1608, assigned to email_to at 1718, and passed to wp_mail() at 1592 together with the generated PDF, so anyone can have the server email the converted page to an arbitrary address.

Contributor-written shortcode attributes button_indicator_timeout and button_custom_indicator (button_ prefix, copied into $options at lines 943-949) are placed unescaped into $config, then json_encode'd (no JSON_HEX_APOS) and emitted inside the single-quoted onclick attribute at line 713, so a single quote breaks out of the attribute and injects event handlers rendered to every visitor.

Contributor-supplied button_indicator_html attribute is meant to be wp_kses_post-filtered for users without unfiltered_html, but line 930 assigns the sanitized value to button_custom_html instead, so the raw value is stored in $options and echoed unescaped at line 737 when button_indicator is 'html'.

When the admin configures email_recipient 'prompt' and button_disposition 'email', the unauthenticated POST 'recipient' is returned unvalidated (line 1608) as $email_to and passed to wp_mail at line 1592 together with a PDF generated from a same-host URL, so anyone can make the site send that content to an arbitrary address with no capability or nonce check.

The unauthenticated POST 'cdata' (line 1673) is accepted for content-mode conversion when its check passes; the check uses a token and date index that are present in the page's enc_data (create_button, lines 847-850), and the XOR scheme is publicly reproducible, so an attacker can forge valid content and have the site's converter account render arbitrary HTML.

A contributor-authored [save_as_pdf_pdfcrowd] attachments attribute (also data_file, file, page_background and similar keys) goes into custom_options, is AES-encrypted into the page, and is decrypted by the nopriv AJAX handler for any visitor. prepare_conv() splits attachments on ';' into $files, and build_body() passes each value to file_get_contents() with no base-directory or realpath check, so the file contents are sent to the converter and embedded in the returned PDF.

A contributor-authored shortcode with url and conversion_mode="upload" (or "development") sets those keys in the encrypted payload. The nopriv handler decrypts it and merges it into $options, and do_post_request() calls wp_remote_get($options['url']) with no scheme, host or IP validation (not wp_safe_remote_get) and with redirects followed. The fetched body is converted and returned to the visitor. A second source, POST location, reaches the same sink when the site's conversion_mode is 'auto', with only a host-name check against the permalink.

A contributor-authored shortcode with button_indicator_html and button_indicator="html" reaches eval_shortcode. For authors without unfiltered_html, the sanitisation branch at 929-932 applies wp_kses_post to button_custom_html instead of button_indicator_html, so button_indicator_html stays raw. It is then concatenated into the button markup at create_button_from_style lines 736-737 and rendered to every visitor.

POST location becomes $options['url'] when the URL is on the permalink's host. get_url() fetches it, and when throw_on_400 is set (fail_on_main_url_error or fail_on_any_url_error) and the response status is 400 or higher, it interpolates $url unescaped into HTML in the message at 1018-1019 and 1022. That message is echoed unescaped by get_error_page() at save_as_pdf_pdfcrowd line 1742. This needs a non-default setting, which an admin or a shortcode attribute can enable.

The output_name attribute, which a contributor can set, passes through get_output_name() unsanitised at lines 1062-1063. In email disposition, send_email() calls make_temporary_file($file_name), which concatenates it into $tmp_dir . '/' . $prefix . $file_name and calls fopen(..., 'x') at 1518. This creates a new file outside the temp directory with PDF bytes, which is then deleted after the mail step. Only files that do not already exist are touched.

A contributor's shortcode attribute button_indicator_html (copied into $options at lines 943-949) is meant to be wp_kses_post-filtered for non-unfiltered_html authors, but lines 929-932 write the sanitized value into $attrs['button_custom_html'] instead, so button_indicator_html reaches create_button unsanitized and is concatenated raw into the button markup at line 737 and rendered to all visitors; WordPress kses filtering of post_content on save may limit which markup survives.

A contributor-set url attribute, with fail_on_main_url_error planted to 1, reaches get_url as $url (do_post_request line 1191); when the remote response status is 400 or higher, $url is interpolated unescaped into an HTML href and text node at lines 1018-1019, the message is returned via check_error and echoed unescaped at line 1742 (get_error_page) to any visitor who triggers the conversion.

A contributor's shortcode attribute button_text is copied into $options (lines 943-949) and returned unescaped by get_button_text (lines 534-540) into $button_content (lines 716-726), which is concatenated into the button markup at line 740 and returned at line 749 without any escaping or kses filtering; WordPress kses filtering of post_content on save is the main barrier, so exploitability is uncertain.

Attacker-supplied redirect_uri (any https URL) is sanitised in OAuth\Server and checked only by validate_redirect_uri, which returns true for any https URI when the client is the admin-configured static client (is_static, no registered list); authorize_post then redirects the authorization code to that URI (Server.php:191-193), so a victim who approves the consent screen leaks the code, and without a client secret it is redeemable with the attacker's PKCE verifier.

A contributor stores an arbitrary non-underscore meta string on their own post via wp_update_post_meta (sanitize_text_field keeps serialized-looking strings); wp_duplicate_post reads it with get_post_meta and passes each value to maybe_unserialize() at line 1445, so a crafted serialized object is unserialized server-side, with exploitation depending on available gadget classes.

Same source as the wp_duplicate_post case: a contributor-controlled non-underscore meta string written with wp_update_post_meta is read by get_post_meta at line 2245 and passed to maybe_unserialize() at line 2248 when the page is duplicated, with the same gadget dependency.

tools/call arguments id/status -> execute_tool case wp_update_post checks only edit_post on the target -> sanitize_text_field(status) is written to post_status and wp_update_post runs with no publish_posts check, unlike wp_create_post, so a contributor can publish or schedule their own drafts.

tools/call wp_update_post_meta stores a sanitize_text_field'd string that can contain serialized PHP (lines 1888-1891) -> later get_post_meta at line 1881 (or 1442 in wp_duplicate_post) applies maybe_unserialize to that stored value -> unserialize runs on attacker-chosen data. Exploitation needs a gadget chain in the loaded code, which was not verified.

Bearer token gives the caller's user (Server.php:349-364). The only gate is edit_post on the target post (1396). args['status'] is taken verbatim into post_status (1400) and passed to wp_update_post (1402) with no publish_posts check, so a contributor can publish or schedule their own drafts, bypassing editorial review. Only wp_create_post (1379) checks publish_posts.

redirect_uri comes from $_GET/$_POST (OAuth/Server.php:103, 160) and is checked by validate_redirect_uri. For the static client, get_client returns redirect_uris=[] and is_static=true (Token_Store.php:270-281), so line 290 returns true for any https or localhost URI. authorize_post then issues an auth code and redirects to it (Server.php:191-193). A victim who is logged in and clicks Allow sends the code to an attacker-chosen host.

The filter reads REQUEST_URI (line 157). If the URI merely contains the substring 'bcs-mcp/v1' (line 158), it returns null (line 159), clearing any authentication error another plugin set. This bypasses site-wide REST lockdowns for unrelated core or third-party routes that match the substring. Their own permission callbacks still apply.

$args['key'] (sanitize_text_field) and $args['value'] -> update_post_meta() on a post the caller can edit; there is no protected-meta (underscore-prefixed) or allowlist check, so a contributor can write internal core and plugin meta keys on their own posts.

Post meta values written through wp_update_post_meta (sanitize_text_field keeps serialized strings intact) are read by get_post_meta() and passed to maybe_unserialize() before add_post_meta() in wp_duplicate_post, so a serialized object string stored by the caller is unserialized on duplication; exploitability depends on available gadget classes.

$_REQUEST['id'] -> (int) cast -> get_email() loads any newsletter row by id with no ownership or capability check -> echo $email->message unescaped in the AJAX response; no nonce or capability check guards the handler, so drafts and private email bodies of any id are returned to any logged-in user.

$_REQUEST['id'] -> sanitize_key -> is_numeric branch -> get_email($id) loads any email row without authorization -> NewsletterComposer::regenerate($email) -> wp_send_json_success returns extract_body($email), extract_composer_options($email) and $email->subject; no nonce or capability check on the handler.

$_REQUEST['redirect'] is passed through esc_url_raw() and then checked only with strpos($url, home_url()) !== 0, which accepts any host that merely starts with the site URL (e.g. the site URL followed by an attacker-controlled domain suffix). The value then reaches wp_redirect($url) at line 207.

$_GET['id'] is cast to int and passed to get_email_field($id,'message'). No status, private flag or capability check is applied, so the embedded <style> content of any email, including drafts, is echoed as text/css at line 251.

$_REQUEST['redirect'] -> esc_url_raw (line 196) -> prefix-only check strpos($url, home_url()) !== 0 (line 200), which accepts hosts such as home_url().'.attacker.tld' -> wp_redirect($url) (line 207). The list change at line 198 runs before the check, and the antibot check at line 174 only requires a POST with a recent ts value.

$_REQUEST['redirect'] -> esc_url_raw() -> $url, then the only check is strpos($url, home_url()) !== 0, which is a prefix match, so a host such as home_url().attacker-domain passes -> wp_redirect($url) at line 207. The redirect is reached after the antibot POST check and a valid confirmed _trusted subscriber token, and set_user_list() runs before the check.

Guest checkout billing fields (get_billing_first_name/last_name/company/address_1/address_2/city/postcode, read at lines 1782-1790) are concatenated with '
' at line 1804 with no HTML escaping, then str_replace'd into the document HTML (class-customizer.php replace_placeholders) and echoed unescaped by print_it (packinglist.php:377) to a browser of an admin or the mail-link recipient. Standard WooCommerce checkout may strip tags via wc_clean, so exploitability depends on whether orders can be created without that sanitisation (needs dynamic check).

Request params 'post' (base64 order id) and 'email' (base64 billing email) -> wf_decode (plain base64, no secret) -> wc_get_order -> 'email' compared to billing email at line 1149 as the only check when no access_key is supplied, so a guest who knows an order's billing email can render that order's invoice/packing slip PDF (includes PII); the guest branch at line 1177 skips the ownership/vendor check entirely when get_current_user_id() is 0. Only reachable when wt_pklist_print_button_access_for is not 'logged_in' (default is 'logged_in', which requires login and a nonce).

Customer note set at checkout passes wp_kses_post (class-customizer.php:1452-1457, which keeps img src) and replace_placeholders (customizer.php:1283), then convert_images_to_base64 (customizer.php:1289, 1769-1777) extracts img src and, for http/https URLs, file_get_contents fetches it server-side with no host or IP restriction, embedding image responses in the PDF.
